purpose: Move beyond synthetic reward generation by executing a committed byte-parser target, mutating a retained corpus, and rewarding only newly observed target trace features while comparing uniform scheduling, context-free UCB1, and stationary LinUCB.

campaign.reward: 1 iff the executed child input exposes at least one target trace feature not previously seen by that policy in the run; otherwise 0

target.name: framed-record parser harness
target.traceModel: explicit parser branch/state features covering magic bytes, version/flags, declared-length relations, payload token/brace states, and checksum states

interpretationBoundary: This pilot executes committed target code and evolves a real corpus; reward is not sampled from a synthetic probability model.
The target is a small in-repository parser harness, not an external benchmark program or production parser.
Trace features are explicit branch/state markers, not compiler-instrumented AFL++ edge coverage.
The campaign does not run AFL++, libFuzzer, sanitizers, or crash triage and therefore does not establish real-world fault-finding performance.
All policies receive the same run count and execution budget, but corpus evolution causes their later inputs to diverge.
The negative LinUCB point estimates are preserved as an exploratory result; no inferential significance claim is made.
